source_refs.note: Exercise 4.2, Question 9: Values of lambda for which A and B are singular (book page 60).

blocks.prompt: 9. Find the values of \(\lambda\) if \(A\) and \(B\) are singular. \(A = \begin{bmatrix} 4 & 2 & 3 \\ 7 & \lambda & 6 \\ 2 & 3 & 1 \end{bmatrix}\), \(B = \begin{bmatrix} -2 & 4 & 5 \\ 1 & -2 & 1 \\ 2 & \lambda & 0 \end{bmatrix}\)
blocks.explanation:
A singular matrix is a square matrix whose determinant is 0.
So we set \(|A| = 0\) and \(|B| = 0\) and solve each for \(\lambda\).
Plan: expand each determinant (it is linear in \(\lambda\)), equate to 0, solve.
steps:
Given: \(A = \begin{bmatrix} 4 & 2 & 3 \\ 7 & \lambda & 6 \\ 2 & 3 & 1 \end{bmatrix}\), \(B = \begin{bmatrix} -2 & 4 & 5 \\ 1 & -2 & 1 \\ 2 & \lambda & 0 \end{bmatrix}\), both singular.
To find: \(\lambda\) for \(A\) and \(\lambda\) for \(B\).
Method: Singular means \(|A| = 0\). Expand along row 1.

Expand \(|A|\) along row 1
\[|A| = 4(\lambda - 18) - 2(7 - 12) + 3(21 - 2\lambda)\]
\[= 4\lambda - 72 + 10 + 63 - 6\lambda\]
\[= 1 - 2\lambda\]
Why: Minors: \(\lambda \cdot 1 - 6 \cdot 3\), \(7 \cdot 1 - 6 \cdot 2\), \(7 \cdot 3 - \lambda \cdot 2\); signs \(+,\,-,\,+\).

Solve \(|A| = 0\)
\[1 - 2\lambda = 0\]
\[\lambda = \dfrac{1}{2}\]
Why: \(A\) is singular exactly when its determinant is 0.

Check
\[\lambda = \tfrac{1}{2}:\ |A| = 1 - 1 = 0 \;\checkmark\]
\[|B| = 7(-4) + 28 = 0 \;\checkmark\]
Why: Substituting back gives a zero determinant in both cases.
blocks.final_answer: \(A\) is singular for \(\lambda = \frac{1}{2}\); \(B\) is singular for \(\lambda = -4\).
